{"id": "c2863daa-c926-49e3-88f9-9fc11dd25574", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_fmIAS3blu2PzHtMVNJqIPQ", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Hybrid cloud architectures using AWS Direct Connect gateway | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"### Scenario 3: Extend logically segmented routing to on-premises networks for separation between Line of Business (LOB) or tenants\\\\n\\\\nIn this scenario, as depicted in the following diagram (figure 6), a customer has configured four Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRFs) domains on the on-premises routers while using one Direct Connect connection and four Direct Connect gateways with a dedicated Transit Gateway. This creates end-to-end routing segmentation for each LOB. By provisioning separate Direct Connect gateways with their own Transit VIF, logical segmentation can be extended from a single Transit Gateway up to the customer gateway through the Virtual Interface.\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2023/10/28/Segmentation.png)\\\\n\\\\nFigure 6: Multiple Direct Connect gateways and Transit VIFs for traffic isolation\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/hybrid-cloud-architectures-using-aws-direct-connect-gateway/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Hybrid Connectivity to AWS Transit Gateway with AWS Direct Connect\",\"context\":\"## Hybrid connectivity with AWS Direct Connect architecture\\\\n\\\\nThe following steps describe the on-premises to AWS traffic flow:\\\\n\\\\n1. The traffic is routed to the destination through the AWS Direct Connect link.\\\\n\\\\nFor more information about how to create an AWS Direct Connect connection, see Create a Direct Connect dedicated connection\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/reference-architecture-diagrams/latest/hybrid-connectivity-transit-gateway/hybrid-dx.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Advanced hybrid routing scenarios with AWS Cloud WAN and AWS Direct Connect | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"### Scenario 3: Two on-premises locations, with two AWS Direct Connect connections each, associated with two AWS Regions. Each on-premises location advertises the same IP prefixes to AWS, and there is connectivity between on-premises locations.\\\\n\\\\nAdvertising the same summary IP prefix from multiple on-premises locations to AWS creates an \u201canycast\u201d routing setup. The connectivity between on-premises locations is important in this routing scenario, as it ensures traffic can be routed from AWS to on-premises destinations using the nearest AWS Direct Connect Point of Presence (POP). When needed, traffic can traverse the on-premises backbone to reach the final destination.\\\\n\\\\nWe introduce an additional AWS Direct Connect gateway to control how traffic flows from AWS to on premises:\\\\n\\\\n* We advertise 10.0.0.0/8 \u2013 IPv4 and 2001:db8::/32 \u2013 IPv6 from both on-premises locations on all four Transit VIFs. {"id": "10d36a7c-4002-433e-8af0-1df675e2ee63", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Yes — but it depends on how the VIFs are set up and routed:

- **Private VIFs alone won't do it.** A private VIF connects to a single virtual private gateway (VGW)/VPC, and traffic between two private VIFs doesn't route to each other by default — there's no path for site-to-site traffic through a VGW.
- **Transit VIFs + Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway does work.** If each on-premises site connects via a Transit VIF to a Direct Connect Gateway, and that gateway is associated with a Transit Gateway, the Transit Gateway can route traffic between the two sites (it acts as the hub). This is the standard hybrid connectivity pattern AWS documents for site-to-site communication through AWS.
- **You can also segment or combine behavior.** AWS's hybrid architectures let you use separate Direct Connect Gateways per VIF for traffic isolation between sites, or a shared one if you want them to reach each other — so this is a deliberate routing decision, not automatic.

So the short answer: two private VIFs by themselves — no. Two sites on Transit VIFs tied into the same Direct Connect Gateway/Transit Gateway — yes, AWS becomes the transit hub between them.

Want me to walk through what this would look like for your specific setup (e.g., check your actual Direct Connect/Transit Gateway associations in this account)?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
